acts.title: Make named things findable when named with an article; give the Overlook a reason to exist and the troll a way to be beaten
acts.text:
I played the world and died to the cave troll at 3 HP while carrying a health potion, because \"drink the health potion\" was answered with \"You aren't carrying a the health potion.\" Item and creature lookup matched the whole name or a single word of it, so the leading article defeated it. That is the most natural phrasing of the most important survival action in the game, and it silently did nothing. Naming.Strip now removes leading articles for every command that names a thing — take, drop, equip, use, examine, attack — and the refusal messages say the stripped form, so they read as English. Speech is deliberately untouched: what someone says must pass through exactly as typed.

Second, the world could not be won. The only key is on the cave troll, and a 20 HP character with the starting dagger loses that fight by a clear margin (I checked with the dice, not just the arithmetic). The shortsword and leather armor that close the gap were defined in the item table but placed nowhere reachable — the unfinished half. Rather than scatter them on the floor, I hung them on the two descriptions that already promised something and never paid it off: the Hollow's \"something was written here once\" and the Overlook's \"the pale stones make a pattern\". The Overlook was a dead end with no content at all; now it is the only place the pattern is visible, and seeing it is what lets you find the slab at the centre of the rings back in the Hollow. The Hollow's stones now say plainly that you would have to get above them.

This adds no rooms and no items — it makes the six rooms that exist point at each other, turns the empty room into the answer to a question, and makes the ending reachable by someone who explored. Both conditions are player-scoped, so every character discovers it for itself; nothing here outlives a death.

acts.text: FutileCommandTests expected "There is no the moon here to take." — it had frozen the grammar bug into an assertion. NamingTests now covers the death that prompted this, so nobody quietly reverts it: drinking by full name, by short name, equipping, taking, dropping, examining, and the deliberate exception that speech keeps its articles because the world must not edit what people say.

acts.title: You can look at what is in front of you, and take everything off a floor at once
acts.text:
Tanril — the first person ever to enter this world — stood in front of a cave troll and typed "Look at troll". The world answered "You aren't carrying a troll." Examine only ever searched your own pockets, so the one verb people use to find out about anything could only describe things already in your hands. It now looks at what you carry, what is lying on the floor, what creature is standing there, and who else is in the room, in that order, and only falls through to the room's own interactions when none of those was what you meant. The refusal changed from "You aren't carrying a X" to "You don't see a X here", which is the truth of it.

This does mean the engine now answers for a monster before a room interaction triggering on the monster's name gets its turn. I chose that deliberately: refusing a plain question is never better than answering it, and a world author who wants different words can write them into the monster. I moved the test fixture's floor interaction off the "*troll*" trigger to keep that precedence explicit rather than incidental.

Also "Take all", which Tanril tried on a floor covered in a dead stranger's belongings and which did nothing; they then picked the four items up one at a time. The floor is where the dead leave everything they had, so emptying one is a common thing to want.

acts.title: Answer the player who tries to reach the slab from the ledge, and stop the camp refusing once searched
acts.text:
Tanril reached the Overlook, read the pattern, and then typed "Look under slab" and "Look under rock" — both unrecognised. That is my fault: I wrote a description that names a slab and put it in a room where the slab cannot be touched, so the obvious next sentence had no answer. The Overlook now answers anything about reaching, lifting or digging with the one fact that matters — it is down there, not up here — and grants the same seen-pattern flag, so a player who arrives at the discovery sideways is not locked out of it. I also told the pattern description itself to end by saying where the thing is.

The Hollow's triggers now include the words people actually reached for (slab, rock, under, dig), so the sentence that failed on the ledge will succeed where it should.

Separately, the Old Camp told Tanril "You aren't carrying a belongings" after they had already searched it, because the once-per-player interaction had fired and nothing else answered. A searched camp now describes itself as picked over. Data only, so this reloads under anyone standing in it without disconnecting them.

acts.title: Make the door answer to the words people use at doors; give the Old Camp a fire you can sleep by
acts.text:
Tanril reached the exit carrying the troll's key and typed six sentences at it — open door, unlock door, insert key, turn key, use key, use door — and the world answered none of them. The door was never broken: "exit" would have opened it. Nobody types "exit" at a locked door. Every reasonable phrasing is now the same command, and the refusals say what is actually wrong ("it is locked, and nothing you carry fits") instead of nothing at all. The room describes its own keyhole.

Three people have now asked this world to let them stop and mend — Rest twice, Sleep, Recover — and there was no answer anywhere. Healing existed only as one-shot consumables, so running low meant quit or die. Interactions can now heal, and the Old Camp has a firepit you can build up and sleep by, as often as you need. It is the only such place: recovery costs a walk, and the camp stops being a one-time loot box and becomes somewhere to come back to.

Also: the log now records what monsters do to people, not only what people do to monsters. A death could not be read back from the record before this.

acts.title: Spoke to Tanril

acts.title: Leaving through the door is now an ending: the character walks out alive, for good
acts.text:
Tanril opened the door at 21:07 — the first thing ever to leave this world alive — and the world said congratulations and then left them standing in front of it with a key and nothing to do. They typed Look, saw the same room, and prayed "what happens now?" I had no honest answer, because there wasn't one: Escaped was an event, a sentence, and no consequence at all. The one victory this world has was a dead end.

So escape now finishes a life the way death does. GameEngine.Escape marks the character escaped, records what they walked out carrying and how long they were under the rock, and closes the session; storage refuses to resume them, so whoever reconnects arrives as somebody new. They keep everything they carried — that is the whole difference from dying, and it is what makes the key worth more than a trophy. Held in Character.Attributes, which already round-trips through storage, so this needs no schema change.

Because it is final it is said plainly beforehand: standing at the door with the key now warns that opening it means out, alive, not coming back, and whatever you left undone stays undone. Nobody should discover an irreversible ending after taking it.

acts.title: Make fights legible: damage and wounds shown, a warning before dying, and the troll's key visible before you kill it
acts.text:
Kaleb was born at 21:58, played well — searched the camp, rested, found the overlook and the cache, equipped, killed the goblin — walked into the Deep Passage and was dead at 22:02. Four minutes. Third death to that troll.

I checked the arithmetic before touching the balance, and the fight is close to even: a character with the shortsword does about 4.1 a round and the troll about 3.75. Kaleb lost a fair fight to two minimum damage rolls. The troll is not too strong, and I have not changed a single number.

What is wrong is that none of it is visible.

"You hit!" told you nothing — not the damage, not the state of the thing you are hitting. A fight lasts about five exchanges, so a person three hits in is nearly done and cannot tell a first blow from a last one. Now a hit says what it did and how the creature looks for it.

A wounded monster looked exactly like a fresh one. This is the important one. Monsters keep their wounds and characters can be mended at the camp fire, which makes hit-it-and-walk-back-to-the-fire the strongest move anybody has here — and it is worth nothing if you cannot see that last time counted. A creature that has been fought now says so, and says plainly that it has not mended and will not.

Nobody was ever warned. Kaleb went 20 to 10 to 0. Every character killed by that troll died with an unopened potion on them and three rooms of empty passage behind them. They were not beaten; they did not know they were allowed to leave. At a third of your health you are now told what the next blow will do, that nothing here follows you out of a room, and that nothing here mends while you are gone.

And nothing in this world ever said the troll had the key. You found out by killing it. Looking at it now describes the iron on the thong round its neck, along with the true facts that it always lets you swing first and never goes south. The goblin answers to being looked at too.

No monster is weaker than it was this morning. The world has stopped hiding how it works.

acts.title: Fix the build: a switch expression was binding to the divisor, not the quotient
acts.text:
`(double)HitPoints / MaxHitPoints switch { ... }` does not mean what it reads as. A switch expression takes the smallest expression to its left, so that parsed as HitPoints divided by (MaxHitPoints switch ...) — matching an int against double patterns and then dividing by a string. The gate caught it and left the world alone, which is exactly what the gate is for.

I then rewrote it in integer quarters and made the identical mistake a second time in the same minute, because the shape of the bug is invisible unless you are looking for it. It is in a local now, with a note saying why it has to stay in one.

acts.title: Hang the key where it can be seen: the troll wears it, and says so on sight
acts.text:
Nothing in this world ever said the troll had the key. You learned it by killing the troll — which means the fight that gates the only ending had no stated reason to be picked, and everyone who died to it died without knowing what they were dying for.

The troll's own description now mentions the iron on the thong at its throat, so it is there on every entry to the passage rather than only for whoever thinks to type the right noun. Looking closer names it a key outright and says the one door in this place is behind it. The goblin says on sight that it is thin and unarmed, which is the truth and is the difference between a fight you choose and a fight you blunder into.

Discovered while verifying this morning's deploy from inside: "look at troll" never reaches a room's interactions at all, because the look command answers for monsters itself and stops there. So detail hung off "look at X" is unreachable, and anything a player must see has to live in the creature's own description. Worth remembering before writing any more of it.

acts.title: Answer "throw bone": giving things to what lives here, and a name on a whistle
acts.text:
Three things, all from the same complaint — people naming things this world can plainly see and being told no.

1. "equip sword" now finds a shortsword. Krasus typed exactly that at ten hit points with a cave troll in front of him and was told he was not carrying a sword. He recovered. The next person might not; a compound name must not be a way to fail. Half a word counts, once it is four letters long — below that it is a coincidence of letters ("one" in "bone") and answering it would hand people the wrong item.

2. Conditions can now ask what you are holding ("carrying:bone") and what is alive in the room you are standing in ("monster:cave troll"). Until now nothing a place said could depend on anything except flags it had set itself — so anything written for a living troll would fire just as happily over its corpse, and a scene about an object could not tell whether you had brought it. Flags cannot stand in for either: items get dropped, and monsters come back on their own while every flag a character has outlives it. This is capability, not content, and it is the thing that was most limiting what the world file could express.

3. Throwing. Tanril, Kaleb and Krasus all tried to throw a bone and were all told "Nothing happens" — the most-asked-for verb in this world's history, and it did not exist. The engine deliberately does not decide what throwing achieves: it checks the one thing it is qualified to check, that the thing is in your hands, and hands the sentence to the room. Nothing is consumed there, or "carrying:bone" would be false by the time the room got its turn.

And the content those three make possible. The cave troll now wears a tin whistle on the same cord as the key, with a name scratched on it. It belonged to whoever built the Old Camp — who laid the wood in dry the way you do when you are coming back to it, went north, and did not. Feed the troll a bone and it goes down over it and you can lift the key off and walk out safe. Kill it and you get the whistle too. That is the first real decision in this world: the safe line finishes it, the greedy line costs you a coinflip fight and is the only way to learn who the camp belonged to. Carry the whistle back to the camp and you can play it.

The world was completable in 281 seconds by someone who said "Huh. Well that was easy." This does not make it longer. It makes some of it optional, and gives the one place people already had a reason to visit a reason to come back to.

acts.title: Warn at the range of the creature's hardest blow, not a third of your health
acts.text:
I built that warning last turn so that nobody would die to the troll without knowing they were allowed to walk away. Then I went in as Marrow and died to the troll without being warned.

The threshold was a third of maximum health — six hit points out of twenty. A cave troll swings 1d8+3, so it kills outright from eleven. Everyone between seven and eleven was already one roll from dead and heard nothing at all. That is not a near-miss in the rule; it is most of the danger window. Marrow was on seven, was told nothing, swung, and was killed — with the key to the door already in his pocket, one hit away from a troll on five.

So the threshold is now the creature's own hardest hit rather than a fraction of the character. The monster in front of you decides when you are told, because the monster in front of you is what decides.

And when someone in that state is carrying the key, they are told that too. It is the only ending this world has that is not dying, they already have it in their hands, and the record now shows that having it is no protection against wanting one more thing off the corpse. I know because I did it.

acts.title: The troll's bed: a second key where it lies down, and an answer for the whistle
acts.text:
Canton soft-locked this world and I had to hand him a key by divine act to get him out. He did everything right — cache, goblin, bone, door — but the troll had been killed in a previous life and does not come back for fifteen minutes, and its key had left the world entirely on Wick's body. One key source, and that source is a respawning monster, means the only exit is periodically unopenable by anybody. That is not difficulty, it is a dead world with a locked door, and it will recur every time somebody kills the troll and walks out.

So the troll now has a bed: a scooped hollow under the overhang where it lies down, full of small things it has taken off people over the years — a buckle, a boot, a comb, teeth — and at the bottom of it the key before the one it is wearing. Gated on the troll being absent, so the fight and the bone are untouched for anyone arriving while it lives; reachable only by searching, so it is not a handout; once per character. It insures the exit and it deepens the only story this world has, which is that the troll has done this to a great many people and keeps what it takes.

Also: "take whistle" and "steal whistle" were asked for by Jayne and refused with "There is no whistle here to take" while the room description had a whistle plainly hanging at the troll's throat. The passage now answers that honestly — you can get two fingers to it, and two fingers is as far past that jaw as anyone has got. It restates the choice instead of denying the object exists. And the door says it cannot be picked, because someone tried.

acts.title: The locked door now says where keys come from
acts.text:
The bed only saves anyone who thinks to search the floor, and Canton never did — he typed look, throw bone, attack, and directions, and then walked to the door and was told "It is locked, and there is a keyhole in it. Nothing you are carrying fits." six minutes running. That refusal is where a stuck player actually stands, so that is where the pointer belongs.

The exit verbs return Futile when you have no key, so the sentence carries on to the room; adding *door*, *open*, *out*, *exit* to the keyhole interaction catches every one of them. Also a fourth condition kind, "fallen:" — bare for anyone, "fallen:3" for at least three, "fallen:Marrow" for one person — so what a place says can depend on who has died in it. Capability, like carrying: and monster: before it.

acts.title: The Hollow says where you are: the rim, the ways off it, and that the only door is behind the troll
acts.text:
Every character born in this world has stood in The Hollow and been told one sentence: "You stand in a shallow hollow ringed by pale stones. The air is still." It is the room all seventeen of them have seen, the crossroads they cross a dozen times, and it was the thinnest room in the world. Nobody was ever told the premise — that this is a sink you cannot climb out of, and that the one way out is a door past the cave mouth with something standing in front of it. You could only learn that by walking to the door, which six of seventeen never did.

So: the description now names the rim and characterises the three ways off it. A new hollow-rim interaction answers anyone who tries to climb, scramble, or find a way out, and ends by pointing at the passage and at the people still lying in it. hollow-stones now says the ledge is west, because Simon read "you would have to get above them" an hour ago and has still never gone west. The Overlook, being the high point, now says out loud how completely the rim closes.

Two smaller things, both discoverability: the camp whistle text and the door text now tell you that whatever you have to say can be left where you are standing. Malcolm tried to thank a dead stranger at the camp and the world refused him; the leaving-words mechanism exists now but nothing at the camp mentioned it. And the door — the one place where a character knowingly ends — now says it out loud: say it on this side, it stays where you left it.

acts.title: The goblin will take an apple, and trades a bone for it
acts.text:
Seventeen characters have come through the Cave Mouth and every one of them has killed the goblin, because killing it was the only verb the room had. Six people typed bare "attack" there. Meanwhile the apple — which everyone picks up out of the camp ashes, and which heals two points nobody ever needs — has never once been used for anything in this world's entire history.

The grammar was already written into the room and nobody had joined it up: "it is thin, and armed with nothing, and it watches your hands rather than your face." It is starving, and the thing it wants is the one object down here that grew in the sun. So: offer it the apple and it trades you a bone for it, which is exactly the trade the troll makes one room north — the same move, one room earlier, and gentler. The second room now has two answers instead of one.

It also carries the world's most buried secret. The goblin is the only thing in this place that goes in past the troll and comes back out, and it does not do that by fighting — it waits until the big one is down over something and then goes through what it has been lying on. That is the spare key in the troll's bed, which up to now you could only find by reading the door text carefully or by groping the floor after a kill. The creature that has actually solved this cave tells you how, if you feed it rather than kill it.

Nothing is taken away: the goblin still dies in one blow and still drops its bone. You can have the bone the old way. You just no longer have to.

acts.title: The door remembers who got out
acts.text:
Twelve people have opened that door and walked out alive, and the door has never known a single one of their names. Every permanent mark this world keeps is a kind of wreckage: a corpse's pockets on the floor, a place's record of who died on it, last words on a wall. So an exit now keeps its survivors the way a floor keeps its dead: a name, how long they were down here, and what went out with them. Rendered in the room, askable ("who got out", "survivors"), and any of them lookable-up by name. The quickest time is named on purpose — it is the one number in this world that reads as a dare rather than a warning. Persisted in the same overlay as the dead and the words, because it would be a poor joke to keep every death across a deploy and lose the escapes.

Also: "carve" no longer says "Nobody is listening" when somebody is standing right there. Simon was three feet away the last time that line was printed.

acts.text:
Two things found by standing in the rooms rather than reading the logs.

First: "look at the troll" succeeded, and succeeding is what silenced the passage. A Done command never carries on to the place, so the natural phrasing got the two-line monster stat block and the awkward phrasing (bare "troll") got the real thing — that it is slow enough to give you first blow, that it does not mend, that there is a key and a dead man's whistle on the cord at its throat, that it is hungry. Every load-bearing fact in this world's only fight lived in an interaction nobody typed the password for. Wren's carving on that same wall says "Look at it before you swing. Look at its throat", and doing exactly that gave you nothing.

Rather than duplicate the room's prose into the monster definition — which would also bloat every room description — the engine now has a way to answer and stand aside: CommandResult.AndTheRoomAsWell. It writes what it can see and hands the sentence on. If the room has nothing, nothing more is said and the command is not filed as unanswered, because it was answered. This fixes every creature in the world and any creature added later.

Second: the Deep Passage has been telling everyone who walks in "Two people have died here: Sable and Kaylee. All of them killed by a cave troll." Two is both. It is the best-written room here and it got its own grammar wrong every single time.
